questions.q: Per this lesson's six-step process, what should come first when building a dictionary?
options: Delete all existing tables and start over
Hire an outside consultant before touching any table
Pull the schema using INFORMATION_SCHEMA, rather than starting from a blank spreadsheet
Write marketing copy describing the database
questions.explain: Starting from the real, live schema means you're documenting actual columns with real structural facts for free, instead of guessing what might exist.

questions.q: Which tables does this lesson say should be prioritized when facing an entire database with hundreds of tables?
options: Tables in strict alphabetical order, regardless of usage
Tables with the fewest columns, to finish quickly
Only tables created in the last 24 hours
Tables referenced in existing reports and dashboards, then the most confusingly named ones
questions.explain: A table five reports depend on matters more right now than a table nobody has queried in two years — usage and confusion drive the priority order, not alphabetical convenience.

questions.q: In the worked mini-dictionary for dbo.Customer, which column is explicitly linked to a business glossary term?
options: IsActiveFlag, linked to 'Active Customer'
LastPurchaseDate, linked to 'Churn'
None of the three columns have a glossary link
CustomerId, linked to 'Net Revenue'
questions.explain: IsActiveFlag implements the 'Active Customer' concept from the glossary, so the worked example links the two together, per Lesson 11's glossary-dictionary pattern.

questions.q: According to this lesson, is a small, real three-column dictionary better or worse than an unfinished hundred-table one?
options: Worse — a dictionary is useless unless it covers every table in the database
Better — a real, trustworthy small dictionary beats an aspirational, half-finished large one
It depends entirely on which database vendor is being used
Equal — the number of columns documented has no effect on trustworthiness
questions.explain: This mirrors the glossary-building lesson's advice (Lesson 10): scope matters less than completeness and trustworthiness within that scope.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which standards from Lesson 13 should be enforced while writing dictionary descriptions?
options: Only that descriptions be under 10 words
Only that descriptions be written in a foreign language
No standards apply during the building process — they only apply after publishing
Naming compliance, mandatory description coverage, and terminology consistency with the glossary
questions.explain: Step 3 explicitly calls for enforcing Lesson 13's three standards while writing descriptions, not as an afterthought applied later.
